## 6 · In one year, how much are the five biggest tech companies spending on AI infrastructure?

<sub>**1** — QUESTION 1 OF 10</sub>

**A** — About $80 billion

**C** — About $800 billion

## 7 · In one year, how much are the five biggest tech companies spending on AI infrastructure?

<sub>**1** — QUESTION 1 OF 10</sub>

**A** — About $80 billion  
**B** — About $250 billion  
**C** — About $800 billion  
THE ANSWER  ·  C  
About $800 billion — in 2026 alone.  Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, in twelve months — nearly double what they spent in 2025, and more than fifteen times Nepal’s entire annual economy. And here is the part that matters: none of that money was spent to make your job easier. It was spent building an engine. The capability is already paid for and already sitting in a free browser tab. The bottleneck is no longer the technology. It is whether you know what to ask.  
This connects to  →  AI problem solving — knowing what to ask (Part 2)  

## 8 · An airline’s chatbot invented a discount that didn’t exist. A customer relied on it. Who paid?

<sub>**2** — QUESTION 2 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The customer — it was only a bot  
**B** — The airline, in full  
**C** — The company that built the bot  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 9 · An airline’s chatbot invented a discount that didn’t exist. A customer relied on it. Who paid?

<sub>**2** — QUESTION 2 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The customer — it was only a bot  
**B** — The airline, in full  
**C** — The company that built the bot  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
The airline. In full.  Moffatt v. Air Canada, February 2024. A grieving customer asked the airline’s website chatbot about bereavement fares. It told him he could claim the discount after travelling — the airline’s real policy said otherwise — and he booked on the strength of it. In tribunal, the airline argued the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions. The tribunal called that a remarkable submission and rejected it: a company is responsible for everything on its website, chatbot or not. Your bot’s words are your words. And notice: nobody hacked anything. It was helpful, and wrong.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — accountability (Part 5)  

## 10 · What does the “GPT” in ChatGPT actually stand for?

<sub>**3** — QUESTION 3 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Generative Pre-trained Text  
**B** — Generative Pre-trained Transformer  
**C** — Generative Predictive Text  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 11 · What does the “GPT” in ChatGPT actually stand for?

<sub>**3** — QUESTION 3 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Generative Pre-trained Text  
**B** — Generative Pre-trained Transformer  
**C** — Generative Predictive Text  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
Generative Pre-trained Transformer.  It’s a prediction engine trained on an enormous amount of text. It generates the next likely word — it does not look up a stored answer. And “Pre-trained” is the word that matters to you: somebody else already spent the hundreds of millions and already read most of the public internet. You are not training anything today. You are hiring something that arrived over-qualified, and with total amnesia about your business.  
This connects to  →  Understanding how AI really works — the base of everything  

## 12 · You ask AI the same question twice, word for word, in two fresh chats. What do you get?

<sub>**4** — QUESTION 4 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The identical answer, both times  
**B** — Two different answers  
**C** — An error the second time  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 13 · You ask AI the same question twice, word for word, in two fresh chats. What do you get?

<sub>**4** — QUESTION 4 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The identical answer, both times  
**B** — Two different answers  
**C** — An error the second time  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
Two different answers.  A calculator looks the answer up — 7 × 8 is 56, every time, forever. AI doesn’t look anything up. It chooses what comes next from a range of plausible options, and it does not always choose the same one. Nothing is broken. But it means you cannot rely on asking well once: a brilliant question on Monday can get a noticeably worse answer on Tuesday from the identical words. So the goal isn’t a good question. It’s building something that gives you a reliable answer every time.  
This connects to  →  Context Engineering (Part 3) — then saving it as an agent (Part 4)  

## 14 · A New York lawyer filed a court brief citing six previous cases, found using ChatGPT. How many were real?

<sub>**5** — QUESTION 5 OF 10</sub>

**A** — All six  
**B** — Four of the six  
**C** — Zero  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 15 · A New York lawyer filed a court brief citing six previous cases, found using ChatGPT. How many were real?

<sub>**5** — QUESTION 5 OF 10</sub>

**A** — All six  
**B** — Four of the six  
**C** — Zero  
THE ANSWER  ·  C  
Zero.  All six were invented — names, citations, quotes, the judges who wrote them. Mata v. Avianca, 2023. When he grew suspicious, he asked ChatGPT whether the cases were real, and it said yes. He was sanctioned $5,000. It did not stop there: more than 2,300 court cases worldwide have now been logged with AI-invented citations, and in 2025 two US federal judges withdrew rulings after their own staff used AI. It produced text that looked exactly like a real citation, because that is what it is built to do. Confidence is not a signal of accuracy.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — judgment and verification (Part 5)  

## 16 · Which workers are most exposed to AI — and which ones gain the most from using it?

<sub>**6** — QUESTION 6 OF 10</sub>

**B** — Office workers exposed — and the LEAST experienced gain most  
**C** — Office workers exposed — and the MOST experienced gain most

## 17 · Which workers are most exposed to AI — and which ones gain the most from using it?

<sub>**6** — QUESTION 6 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Manual and factory workers, on both counts  
**B** — Office workers exposed — and the LEAST experienced gain most  
**C** — Office workers exposed — and the MOST experienced gain most  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
Office workers are most exposed. The least experienced gain the most.  Every previous wave of automation went after routine, physical, predictable work. This one reverses that: exposure is highest in educated, office-based judgement work — analysts, managers, consultants, marketers, writers. In a study of customer support agents using AI, productivity rose about 15% on average — and about 30% for the least experienced. But the same group is where hiring is slowing: in 2025, US employment for 22–25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs fell 13% relative to older colleagues. So: the people most exposed are in this room. The people who gain most, and stand to lose most, are the ones you employ and train.  
This connects to  →  Where you sit in all of this — the AI Pyramid, next

## 19 · AI is not another tool

<sub>THE BIG SHIFT</sub>

Every past technology extended our bodies. This one reaches into how we think.  

## 20 · Each wave of technology extended a different human power

<sub>THE BIG SHIFT</sub>

Machines  
Extended physical strength  
**→** — Computers  
Sped up calculation  
**→** — The Internet  
Connected information  
**→** — AI  
Extends cognitive labour itself  
Writing · summarising · reasoning · ideation · deciding — tasks that were, until recently, only human.  
SO  The bottleneck is no longer what the technology can do. It is whether you know how to work with it.  

## 22 · From AI literacy to AI nativity

<sub>**21** — THE GOAL OF TODAY</sub>

AI LITERACY  
Understanding AI — what it is, what it can do, how it works.  
Prepares you to RECOGNISE AI.  
AI NATIVITY  
Integrating AI fluidly into everyday reasoning, problem-solving and decisions.  
Prepares you to think and work WITH AI.  
“Like the difference between studying a language and speaking it natively.”  
Nativity shows up not in what you KNOW about AI, but in how you HABITUALLY use it.

<sub>**22** — THE CORE IDEA</sub>

A workforce is not uniform — and AI capability shouldn’t be either.  Khatri & Khanal (2026), NAAMII.  

## 24 · How AI capability is distributed 🖼

<sub>**23** — THE FRAMEWORK</sub>

Scan for the paper  
Khatri & Khanal (2026) — The AI Pyramid · arxiv.org/abs/2601.06500  

## 25 · Two things the shape is telling you

<sub>**24** — THE FRAMEWORK</sub>

1 · The base is the most critical layer  
Just as a pyramid needs a broad foundation to hold a narrow peak, an AI-ready organisation needs broad AI-native capability to support its builders and specialists. Without the base, nothing above it works.  
2 · It is NOT a career ladder  
Nobody has to “climb” to the top. The layers describe how capability is spread across a system — not a ranking of people. Everyone needs Native. Only some roles need the rest.  
Nobody in this room is at the bottom of anything. You are in the layer that decides whether the rest of it produces any value.  

## 26 · Frame the task well

<sub>**25** — THE FIVE HABITS  ·  1 OF 5</sub>

Vague in, vague out. Tell AI exactly what you want.  
WEAK PROMPT  
“Write about climate change.”  
STRONG PROMPT  
“Write a 150-word summary of how climate change affects farming in Nepal, for high-school students, in simple language.”  
The habit:  Say who it’s for, how long, what angle, and what format. Specific requests get useful answers.  
This connects to  →  AI problem solving — find the real task first (Part 2)  

## 27 · Give it the right context

<sub>**26** — THE FIVE HABITS  ·  2 OF 5</sub>

AI only knows what you put in front of it. So put the right things in front of it.  
WEAK  
“Is this email okay?”  
(no email, no goal, no audience)  
STRONG  
“Here’s my email [paste it]. Goal: politely decline but keep the relationship. Reader: my manager. Make it shorter and warmer.”  
The habit:  Give it the material, your role, your goal, the audience, and any constraints. Context is the whole game.  
This connects to  →  Context Engineering · Exercise 1 (Part 3)  

## 28 · Verify before you trust

<sub>**27** — THE FIVE HABITS  ·  3 OF 5</sub>

Confident does not mean correct. Treat AI like a fast, clever intern — check its work.  
RISKY HABIT  
Copy-paste the answer and send it. Assume the names, numbers and quotes are real.  
AI-NATIVE HABIT  
Ask “what are your sources?”, cross-check the facts, and be extra sceptical of specific dates, figures and citations.  
The habit:  Plausible ≠ true. Verify anything you’d be embarrassed to get wrong — you own the result.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — judgment (Part 5)  

## 29 · Work it across the whole task

<sub>**28** — THE FIVE HABITS  ·  4 OF 5</sub>

Stop using AI for one-off replies. Run it across the entire job, step by step.  
ONE-OFF USE  
Ask a single question, get a single answer, move on.  
ORCHESTRATED USE  
“Plan a 3-day Pokhara trip: 1) research options, 2) build a day-by-day itinerary, 3) turn it into a budget table.”  
The habit:  Break a goal into steps and let AI carry each one — research, draft, check, format. That is how agents work.  
This connects to  →  Agentic AI · Exercise 2 (Part 4)  

## 30 · Keep judgment — and accountability

<sub>**29** — THE FIVE HABITS  ·  5 OF 5</sub>

AI advises. You decide. The final call, and the responsibility, stay with the human.  
HAND OVER THE WHEEL  
Let AI decide. Paste in private or sensitive data. Blame the tool if it’s wrong.  
STAY IN CHARGE  
Accept, challenge, refine or reject each output. Protect privacy, watch for bias. Own the decision.  
The habit:  Use AI to think better, not to stop thinking. You are accountable for what you act on.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — accountability (Part 5)  

## 31 · AI PROBLEM SOLVING

<sub>PART 2 OF 5</sub>

Find the right problem  
Before you can specify a task well, you have to be sure it is the right task. Five moves, in order, on a problem you actually have.  

## 32 · AI does not solve your problem.

<sub>**31** — THE ONE IDEA FOR THIS PART</sub>

It makes your thinking faster.  
YOU BRING  
The real problem. The people. What has already been tried and failed. What the budget actually is.  
AI BRINGS  
Speed. Ten options instead of two. A structure for your thinking. A first draft you can argue with.  
ONLY YOU DECIDE  
What is realistic here. Who will actually say yes. What is worth doing on Monday.  
Speed without direction is just a faster way to arrive somewhere you did not want to go.  
This connects to  →  Habit 5 — keep judgment and accountability  

## 33 · Five moves, asked in order

<sub>**32** — THE METHOD</sub>

Same problem. Same tool. Five different asks. That is all Part 2 is.  
**1** — DIAGNOSE  
“What is really going on here?”  
Do not ask for solutions yet. Make the AI interrogate the problem until the real cause surfaces.  
**2** — BRAINSTORM  
“What could we possibly do?”  
Ask for volume, not quality. Ten mediocre ideas beat two safe ones at this stage.  
**3** — FILTER  
“What is actually realistic for us?”  
Apply your budget, your constraints, your politics. Split the work: AI, you, or a tool.  
**4** — STRESS-TEST  
“Why would this fail?”  
Make the AI argue against you before the person who matters does it for free.  
**5** — COMMIT  
“What exactly are we doing?”  
One option, one owner, one form of output. The rest goes in a drawer.  
THE ONE RULE  You may not move to the next move until the room can say the current one out loud in a single sentence.  

## 34 · None of these five moves is new

<sub>**33** — WHERE THIS METHOD COMES FROM</sub>

Each one has a well-established ancestor. Knowing which also tells you its known failure mode.  
DIAGNOSE  
Root-cause analysis — 5 Whys, Ishikawa (1968)  
Fails when the first plausible cause is accepted without evidence.  
BRAINSTORM  
Deferred judgment — Osborn (1953); the divergent half of the Double Diamond  
Fails when the group judges while generating, and stops at idea three.  
FILTER  
Function allocation — Fitts’s list / MABA-MABA (1951)  
Fails at the joins between piles, not inside them. Part 4 is about the joins.  
STRESS-TEST  
Pre-mortem (Klein, 2007); red-teaming  
Fails when you argue with yourself instead of letting something else argue.  
COMMIT  
The convergent half of the Double Diamond (Design Council, 2005)  
Fails when a group picks three options and delivers none.  
The AI is not the method. The method is forty years old; the AI just runs it faster and with more patience than a room does.  

## 35 · “Our training sessions are almost empty — especially of the people who most need them.”

<sub>**34** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  WATCH FIRST, THEN YOU DO IT</sub>

— a real problem, in the words somebody would actually use  
NOTICE WHAT THIS IS NOT  
It is not a solution in disguise (“we need a better mailing list”).  
It is not a diagnosis (“people are not interested”).  
It is just the symptom, honestly stated. That is exactly where you should start.  
If your problem statement already contains the answer, you have skipped move 1 and you will not get it back.  

## 36 · Diagnose — make the AI ask YOU questions

<sub>**35** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 1</sub>

WHAT I TYPE  
I run staff training for a mid-sized organisation.  
Problem: attendance at our training sessions is very low, especially among the people whose work it is meant to improve.  
Do NOT suggest solutions yet.  
Ask me 5 questions that would help identify the real root cause.  
WHAT COMES BACK  
1. What time of day are sessions held?  
2. How far must people travel, and how?  
3. Who currently invites people — and how?  
4. Does attending cost them anything they are not reimbursed for?  
5. Has anyone asked the people who did not come, why?  
THE TURN THAT MATTERS  Answering question 1 out loud, the group realises sessions run at 11 AM — exactly when the people they are aimed at are on shift. The problem was never “lack of interest.” It was the clock.  

## 37 · The AI asked. Now you answer — and only then converge.

<sub>**36** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 1, CLOSING THE LOOP</sub>

Five questions are not a diagnosis. The diagnosis is what you say back.  
WHAT I TYPE NEXT  
My answers:  
1. 11 AM, on a weekday.  
2. 30–60 minutes, mostly on foot or bus.  
3. Line managers, verbally, a day before.  
4. Yes — unpaid time.  
5. No. We have never asked them.  
Based ONLY on these answers, give the single most likely root cause, and name the evidence in my answers that supports it. If the evidence is thin, say so.  
WHY THE LAST TWO LINES MATTER  
“Name the evidence” stops it inventing a cause that sounds right.  
“If the evidence is thin, say so” gives it permission to tell you that you have not asked the people who did not come — which is the real finding.  
That is the LIMITS dial. You meet it formally in Part 3.  
The trap:  an AI-generated root cause is a hypothesis, not a finding. Before you act on it, name one thing you could check this week that would prove it wrong.  
This connects to  →  Habit 3 — verify before you trust  

## 38 · Brainstorm — now ask for volume

<sub>**37** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 2</sub>

WHAT I TYPE  
The root cause is timing: sessions run at 11 AM, when the people they are for are on shift.  
Give me 10 different ways to address this. Do not filter for feasibility yet — I want range, including options that change the format, not just the time.  
WHAT COMES BACK (10 OPTIONS; HERE ARE 5)  
1. Move sessions to early evening  
2. Run the same session twice, two slots  
3. Take the session to where people already are  
4. Attach it to a meeting that already happens  
5. Make it asynchronous — record it once  
WHERE GROUPS GO WRONG  They stop at the first good idea. Options 7, 8 and 9 are usually the ones nobody in the room would have said out loud — and one is often the cheapest thing you could do.  

## 39 · Three ways to get past the obvious six

<sub>**38** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 2, PUSHING FURTHER</sub>

The first six ideas are the ones any organisation would try. These three prompts get you the rest.  
CONSTRAIN IT HARD  
“Three of these are things anyone would try. Give me three more that work with no budget, no new staff, and no new software.”  
Constraints force originality. Unconstrained brainstorming returns the average of the internet.  
CHANGE WHO IS ASKING  
“Now answer as somebody who thinks the sessions themselves are the problem, not the timing.”  
A different role produces a different list. This is the ROLE dial, used on purpose.  
ASK A SECOND TOOL  
Paste the same prompt into a different model. Put both lists side by side.  
Where they agree is the safe ground. Where they disagree is worth a conversation.  
KEEP ALL TEN  Do not delete anything yet. Filtering works better with a long list. Add the group’s own ideas to the same sheet, unmarked.  

## 40 · Filter — split the work three ways

<sub>**39** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 3</sub>

Every option you keep gets broken into three piles. This is the most important slide in Part 2.  
AI CAN DO THIS  
• Draft the invitation and the reminder  
• Write the session plan and handouts  
• Summarise feedback from 60 forms  
• Produce a one-page budget note  
• Translate material into another language  
ONLY YOU CAN DO THIS  
• Know that 11 AM does not work here  
• Get the person with the budget to say yes  
• Ask the people who did not come, in person  
• Judge what will offend and what will land  
• Show up on the day and be trusted  
NEEDS A TOOL OR RESOURCE  
• A room available after 5 PM  
• Printed material — no data needed  
• A saved assistant that holds the context  
• Two people to cover the shift  
• A small budget line  
THE TEST  If your “only you” column is empty, you have not understood your own problem yet.  

## 41 · The piles are easy. The joins are not.

<sub>**40** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 3, THE PART EVERYONE GETS WRONG</sub>

Splitting work between people and machines is a 1951 idea. Its known weakness is the handover.  
WHAT THE THREE PILES ASSUME  
That a task comes apart cleanly, and that each piece can be done well on its own.  
Mostly true. Drafting really is separable from deciding.  
WHERE IT ACTUALLY BREAKS  
At the seams. The AI drafts a message using a figure nobody has confirmed. You approve it because it reads well. Neither piece was wrong. The handover was.  
Nobody owns a seam unless somebody is told to.  
So the real question is not “who does what.”  It is: at which handover would a mistake cost the most — and is a named human standing there? Part 4 builds exactly this, and Part 5 makes it a rule.  
This connects to  →  Part 4 — one job per worker, and a human at the expensive join  

## 42 · Stress-test — make it argue against you

<sub>**41** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 4</sub>

You are about to take this to somebody who can say no. Have that conversation here first, for free.  
WHAT I TYPE  
Here is our plan. [paste it]  
I am presenting this to someone who thinks it is a waste of money and time.  
Give me the five strongest objections they will raise, in their words, and for each one the single piece of evidence I would need to answer it.  
Do not defend the plan.  
WHY THIS WORKS  
A pre-mortem beats a review. Asking “is this good?” gets you agreement; asking “why will this fail?” gets you the list.  
“Do not defend the plan” is the line that matters. Without it, the model hands you objections and then rebuts them for you — comfortable and useless.  
The objection you cannot answer is your next piece of work.  
THE RULE  If none of the five objections worries you, you wrote the prompt badly — or you are not being honest about the plan.  

## 43 · Commit — one option, in one form

<sub>**42** — WORKED EXAMPLE  ·  MOVE 5</sub>

First pick ONE option from your shortlist. Then pick ONE form for it. Half-built and real beats fully-planned and imaginary.  
A SAVED ASSISTANT  
A custom AI assistant loaded with your real constraints. You build one of these in Part 4.  
Best if the problem repeats every month.  
A PROMPT PACK  
Four or five tested prompts anyone on your team can reuse: the invitation, the report, the budget note, the follow-up.  
Best if several people need to do this, not just you.  
AN ACTION PLAN  
Five steps, a named owner for each, and dates across the next month — drafted with AI, corrected by you.  
Best if the next move is political rather than technical.  
WHATEVER YOU BUILD, TEST IT ONCE BEFORE YOU STOP  Give it a real task. Generic output means you left your own knowledge out.  

## 44 · Notice what Part 2 just handed you

<sub>**43** — THE HANDOFF</sub>

Not a solution. A specification — and a specification you do not yet know how to write properly.  
FROM MOVE 1  
A root cause you can defend, and the evidence for it  
→  becomes your SOURCE  
FROM MOVE 3  
The list of things AI is actually allowed to do here  
→  becomes your ROLE and your LIMITS  
FROM MOVE 4  
The five objections you have to survive  
→  becomes what you test the output against  
FROM MOVE 5  
One chosen option, in one named form  
→  becomes the thing you build in Part 4  
Part 3 teaches you to write that specification. Part 4 teaches you to stop writing it every time.  

## 45 · Groups of three or four. One real problem. Five moves.

<sub>**44** — NOW YOU</sub>

The value is in the argument around the screen, not in the typing.  
1 · Use any tool you like  
ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude — or all three. Compare them if you want. There is no correct tool.  
2 · One person types, everyone argues  
Rotate who holds the laptop between moves. The typist stops thinking; the arguers do not.  
3 · Write down what surprised you  
You will present it later. The moment where the AI was wrong is often the most useful thing you find.  
4 · Mix backgrounds where you can  
Two people from different teams in one group produce a better argument than two from the same one.  
BEFORE YOU LEAVE MOVE 1  Finish this out loud: “We thought the problem was ______, but the real cause is ______.”  

## 46 · The problem bank

<sub>**45** — PICK ONE</sub>

Choose the one closest to your own situation — or swap in your own version of it. Real beats tidy.  
**A** — The empty room  
Turnout at our training or outreach sessions is very low — especially among the people it is for.  
**B** — No space, no budget  
We cannot get space or a budget line for the thing everyone agrees is a good idea.  
**C** — The unused system  
Staff were given a new digital tool and quietly went back to the old way of doing it.  
**D** — The distrusted platform  
The people we built it for will not use it — they do not trust it with their money or their data.  
**E** — Nobody came  
We announced an event and got nine registrations, six of them our own colleagues.  
**F** — The report nobody reads  
We produce something monthly. We have no evidence anyone has ever acted on it.  
Do not pick the problem you already know how to solve. Pick the one that has been annoying you for months.

## 50 · This is the prompt that made it

<sub>**49** — EXERCISE 1  ·  THE REVEAL</sub>

Use the uploaded photo as the only reference. Transform it into a true 90° top-down drone shot while preserving the exact rider, body proportions, face direction, helmet, riding gear, motorcycle model, color, graphics, accessories, and all visible details. Position the rider naturally lying on the left side of the motorcycle with arms crossed and legs slightly crossed, facing toward the motorcycle. Keep the motorcycle upright on the right side. Add a single white road center line between them on dark wet asphalt. Create a perfectly centered, symmetrical composition with subtle road texture, realistic rain reflections, fine asphalt grain, natural imperfections, soft overcast lighting, realistic shadows, ultra-photorealistic, premium drone photography, 8K. Keep the helmet visor fully closed with a dark smoked/tinted visor. Add a visible motorcycle meter/instrument console exactly matching the original bike’s stock design and perspective. Apply dramatic cinematic color grading with rich contrast, deep blacks, subtle teal-orange tones, and premium high-end visual aesthetics while maintaining realistic colors. Do not add any luggage, saddle bags, top box, or extra accessories to the motorcycle unless they are present in the original reference image. No extra people, vehicles, buildings, text, logos, or watermarks.  
192 words  
For one picture. You wrote about fifteen.  

## 51 · The AI knows nothing about you

<sub>**50** — SO WHAT IS “CONTEXT”?</sub>

Context is everything you put in front of it. It has no memory of you, no access to your files, your company, or your last conversation.  
INSTRUCTION  
What to do.  
“Summarise this.”  “Write me an email.”  “Make it better.”  
CONTEXT  
What to do it with.  
The document. The policy. Your role. Who reads it. What it must look like. What it must never do.  
Most people write 100% instruction and 0% context — then decide the AI is disappointing.  
Your fifteen words were all instruction. The 192 were almost all context.  

## 52 · Five kinds. Every one of them is in that prompt.

<sub>**51** — HOW DO YOU GIVE CONTEXT?</sub>

Nothing technical. Each one is a decision you already know how to make.  
SOURCE  
The material it must work from  
“the uploaded photo as the only reference”  
ROLE  
Who it should be while answering  
“you are an operations analyst”  
SHAPE  
The form the answer must take  
“a true 90° top-down… perfectly centered, symmetrical”  
STYLE  
The register, mood or look  
“soft overcast lighting… deep blacks, subtle teal-orange”  
LIMITS  
What it must never do  
“do not add any luggage… no extra people, text, logos”  
NEXT  You are going to add these five, one at a time, to something far less glamorous than a motorcycle.

## 62 · Round 5 — what to do when something’s missing

<sub>**61** — EXERCISE 1  ·  ROUND 5 OF 5  ·  LIMITS</sub>

The last dial, and the one that keeps you out of trouble.  
SOURCE  
ROLE  
SHAPE  
STYLE  
LIMITS  
WHAT THIS DIAL DOES  
Tells it what to do when the answer is not in the source. Without this, a gap and a fact look identical on the page.  
AND IF YOU SKIP IT  
It fills the gap with something plausible — and plausible is indistinguishable from true at a glance.  
ADD THIS ONE LINE  
If no owner was named, write UNASSIGNED.  
If no date was stated, write NOT STATED.  
If a value is stated twice differently, write BOTH and flag CONFLICT.  
If a topic was raised but not resolved, list it under RAISED BUT NOT DECIDED.  
If you could not hear it, write INAUDIBLE.  
Never fill a gap with something plausible.  
WHAT CHANGES  The gaps become visible and labelled. Now you can see what the AI knew, and what it was guessing.  
In the motorcycle prompt, 33 of the 192 words were rules like these. Saying what you don’t want IS specification.

## 65 · Five rules you can use from tomorrow

<sub>**64** — SO WHAT’S THE RULE?</sub>

Not theory. This is the whole method, and it fits on one slide.  
**1** — Give it the material before you give it the task  
Source first. If it hasn’t seen the thing, nothing else you write will help.  
**2** — Walk the five dials  
Source · Role · Shape · Style · Limits. Ask which one is missing before you rewrite anything.  
**3** — If the answer is wrong, add context — don’t repeat the instruction louder  
“Be more specific” does nothing. Being more specific does everything.  
**4** — Change one thing at a time  
Change five and it improves, you’ve learned nothing — you don’t know which one did it.  
**5** — Say what you don’t want  
A sixth of a professional prompt is “do not”. That’s not negativity, that’s specification.  
AND ONE HABIT  Before you send your next prompt: name three things you left unspecified.

## 69 · A finance worker joined a video call with his CFO and colleagues and made fifteen transfers — $25 million. The CFO was never on the call. What went wrong?

<sub>**7** — QUESTION 7 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The audio was faked, the video was real  
**B** — Every other person on the call was an AI fake  
**C** — Nothing — the CFO stole the money and denied it  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 70 · A finance worker joined a video call with his CFO and colleagues and made fifteen transfers — $25 million. The CFO was never on the call. What went wrong?

<sub>**7** — QUESTION 7 OF 10</sub>

**A** — The audio was faked, the video was real  
**B** — Every other person on the call was an AI fake  
**C** — Nothing — the CFO stole the money and denied it  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
Every other person on that call was generated.  Arup, the engineering firm, Hong Kong office, early 2024. The employee was suspicious of the initial email — so the fraudsters put him on a video call where the CFO and several familiar colleagues all appeared and spoke. Every one was built from video and audio scraped from public conference recordings and past company meetings. Fifteen transfers to five accounts, about US$25 million, and none of it reported recovered. You have all been taught to verify a document. Nobody taught you to verify a face.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — verify before you act (Part 5)  

## 71 · You ask AI to write your company’s new slogan. It gives you one you love. Who owns the copyright?

<sub>**8** — QUESTION 8 OF 10</sub>

**A** — You do — you paid for the tool  
**B** — The AI company does  
**C** — Nobody. It isn’t copyrightable.  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 72 · You ask AI to write your company’s new slogan. It gives you one you love. Who owns the copyright?

<sub>**8** — QUESTION 8 OF 10</sub>

**A** — You do — you paid for the tool  
**B** — The AI company does  
**C** — Nobody. It isn’t copyrightable.  
THE ANSWER  ·  C  
Nobody owns it.  Copyright requires human authorship, so work generated purely by AI cannot be registered — and the US Copyright Office has been explicit that writing the prompt is not enough, because a prompt doesn’t give you control over the expressive result. In March 2026 the US Supreme Court declined to reopen the question. Where a human meaningfully shapes the work, the human parts may be protectable. The AI-generated part is not. So you can use your slogan. You just can’t stop a competitor using it too.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — disclosure and ownership (Part 5)  

## 73 · A major tech company built an AI to score CVs one to five stars, trained on ten years of its own hiring data. What did it start doing?

<sub>**9** — QUESTION 9 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Favouring candidates from expensive universities  
**B** — Downgrading any CV containing the word “women’s”  
**C** — Scoring everyone the same, so it was useless  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 74 · A major tech company built an AI to score CVs one to five stars, trained on ten years of its own hiring data. What did it start doing?

<sub>**9** — QUESTION 9 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Favouring candidates from expensive universities  
**B** — Downgrading any CV containing the word “women’s”  
**C** — Scoring everyone the same, so it was useless  
THE ANSWER  ·  B  
It penalised the word “women’s”.  Amazon. Built from 2014, abandoned by 2015, made public in 2018. It taught itself to downgrade CVs containing “women’s” — as in women’s football team — and marked down graduates of two all-women’s colleges. Nobody programmed that. It learned it, because ten years of tech-industry CVs were mostly from men. Amazon patched those words; the bias reappeared in other forms, so they scrapped the whole thing. And it is not just history: in 2025 a US court let applicants over 40 bring a nationwide age-discrimination case against Workday’s AI screening tools.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — fairness (Part 5, Case 1)  

## 75 · You type your client’s contract into a free AI tool. Is that text used to train the model?

<sub>**10** — QUESTION 10 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Never — that would be illegal  
**B** — Always, in every version  
**C** — It depends which version — and it’s usually a setting  
Which one? Hands up.  

## 76 · You type your client’s contract into a free AI tool. Is that text used to train the model?

<sub>**10** — QUESTION 10 OF 10</sub>

**A** — Never — that would be illegal  
**B** — Always, in every version  
**C** — It depends which version — and it’s usually a setting  
THE ANSWER  ·  C  
It depends, and you can usually change it.  On most consumer tools, personal accounts have used your chats for training unless you switch it off — ChatGPT does by default, and Claude asks you to choose. Gemini split training into its own setting in November 2026. Business, enterprise and API tiers generally do not train on your data. So the answer to “is my data safe” is never yes or no — it is: which tier am I on, and what is the setting? Go and look at yours once. Ninety seconds, and you only do it once.  
This connects to  →  Responsible AI — privacy, before you paste (Part 5)

## 78 · This is the prompt that made it

<sub>THE REVEAL</sub>

A wide-angle, hyper-detailed cinematic photograph of a hidden subterranean library built inside a massive, ancient geo-dome carved into a mountain. The architecture blends ancient ornate Gothic revival style with luminous, organic bioluminescent technology. In the center of the grand chamber, a towering spiral staircase crafted from dark, polished mahogany and brass winds upward toward a massive stained-glass skylight, through which ethereal beams of soft moonlight stream down, cutting through a delicate haze of swirling golden dust motes. The expansive curved walls are lined with infinitely tall, arching bookshelves stuffed with weathered leather-bound tomes, glowing crystalline scrolls, and antique brass astrolabes. A young scholar with bronze skin and dark, braided hair stands on an elevated wooden balcony near the foreground, wearing an intricate velvet coat adorned with fine gold embroidery. They are leaning over a heavy oak desk littered with open maps, glowing alchemical diagrams, magnifying glasses, and half-unrolled parchment. The scholar holds a small, glowing mechanical compass that projects a soft, holographic star map into the air around their hands, illuminating their focused, awe-struck expression. Lush, iridescent blue and violet moss grows along the stone pillars, casting an ambient, romantic glow across the floor. Floating spherical lanterns made of blown glass and brass drift lazily throughout the air, casting warm amber highlights on the rustic stone floor. In the background, deep shadows hint at hidden passageways, forgotten artifacts, and glowing aquariums built into the stone walls filled with bioluminescent deep-sea flora. Shot on a 35mm lens with a shallow depth of field, establishing a grand sense of scale and atmosphere. Cinematic lighting with strong chiaroscuro contrast between the cool moonlight, warm lantern light, and vibrant bioluminescence. Rich textures of polished wood, tarnished metal, weathered paper, and rough stone captured in crisp 8k resolution.  
302 words  
Find the five dials in it: Source · Role · Shape · Style · Limits.

## 103 · One job per worker

<sub>**102** — RULE 1 OF 2</sub>

WHAT PEOPLE TRY FIRST  
One assistant that reads the meeting, writes the messages, checks them, and knows the policy.  
It does all four jobs badly, and you can never tell which one failed.  
WHAT YOU DID INSTEAD  
Three workers. One job each. Each one testable on its own.  
When something goes wrong you know exactly which worker to fix — and fixing it doesn’t break the other two.  
SO  An assistant for everything is an assistant for nothing.  

## 104 · Short chains beat clever ones

<sub>**103** — RULE 2 OF 2</sub>

Because the chain is always worse than any step in it.  
**90%** — one worker, on its own  
**81%** — two workers, joined  
**73%** — three workers, joined  
Every worker you add multiplies the error, it doesn’t add to it. Three good workers make a mediocre chain.  
WHICH IS WHY  Keep the chain short, and put the human at the join that costs the most to get wrong.  

## 105 · Where this pays off

<sub>**106** — WHY IT MATTERS</sub>

IN ANY ORGANISATION  
Any process that goes read → write → check is now three saved workers instead of somebody’s Monday morning.  
And it survives that person being on leave, because the job description is saved, not remembered.  
IN NEPAL, SPECIFICALLY  
A six-person firm in Kathmandu can now answer at the speed of a forty-person one — and the tone-and-language judgement that used to sit in one bilingual person’s head is written down.  
No engineers. No spend. A browser tab.  
You didn’t build software today. You wrote three job descriptions.  
Habit 4 · Work it across the whole task  
This connects to  →  Part 5 — who is allowed to decide what  

## 106 · NO EXERCISE FOR THIS ONE

<sub>PART 5 OF 5</sub>

Responsible AI  
Own it. You don’t practise this in a sandbox. You practise it every day, in decisions that already have your name on them.  

## 107 · AI moved the work.

<sub>**108** — THE LAST PART</sub>

It didn’t move the responsibility.  
The tribunal didn’t care that a chatbot wrote it. And you put a human at the end of your chain in Part 4 for exactly that reason.  

## 108 · The algorithm that took a widow’s rations

<sub>**109** — CASE 1 OF 5</sub>

WHAT HAPPENED  
Telangana, India, used an algorithm called Samagra Vedika to decide who could keep a food-ration card. It matched Bismillah Bee’s late husband, a rickshaw puller, to a different man who owned a car — and her family’s card was cancelled. Officials were meant to check every result before acting. In practice, they took the algorithm’s word.  
WHAT IT COST  
More than 1.86 million ration cards cancelled between 2014 and 2019, and 142,086 new applications rejected, without notice. When the Supreme Court ordered a recheck, 15,471 of the first 205,734 cards reviewed were restored. Bismillah Bee went more than seven years without rations. The state says its error rate is under 5%.  
WHAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT  
A named official required to check the person’s actual records before any “deny” — treating the algorithm’s output as a lead, not a verdict.  
Nobody chose to be unfair. A bad data match and a rubber stamp were enough.  
Al Jazeera / Pulitzer Center investigation, January 2024 · Amnesty International, April 2024  

## 109 · The national AI policy with fake sources

<sub>**110** — CASE 2 OF 5</sub>

WHAT HAPPENED  
South Africa’s communications department drafted the country’s national AI policy. Cabinet approved it in March 2026 and published it for public comment. Journalists then checked the reference list: at least six of its 67 sources did not exist. The minister said the most plausible explanation was AI-generated citations that nobody had checked.  
WHAT IT COST  
The minister withdrew the whole policy in April 2026, said it had compromised its integrity and credibility, and promised consequences for the drafters and reviewers. Public consultation had to start again. A national AI policy was undone by the exact failure it was written to govern.  
WHAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT  
Opening one citation. Not all of them — one, chosen at random, is enough to find the problem.  
A Cabinet approval sat on a reference list nobody had opened.  
Reuters and Mail & Guardian, April 2026 · draft withdrawn by South Africa’s Minister of Communications  
This is the closest case to your own desk. Nobody was reckless. Somebody was busy.  

## 110 · The face that was never there

<sub>**111** — CASE 3 OF 5</sub>

WHAT HAPPENED  
Rite Aid ran facial recognition across hundreds of US stores to identify suspected shoplifters. The regulator found it generated thousands of false matches, that it performed worst on women and on Black, Asian and Latino shoppers, and that the staff acting on its alerts were never told how often it was wrong.  
WHAT IT COST  
Customers were followed, searched and accused in front of other shoppers. Some of them were children. A five-year ban on using facial recognition at all, plus mandatory deletion of the images and every model built from them. Rite Aid has since closed every store, after a second bankruptcy in 2025.  
WHAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT  
Testing who the system fails on before deploying it — and telling the people acting on its output what its error rate is.  
A tool with no stated error rate cannot be used responsibly by anybody.  
US Federal Trade Commission enforcement action, December 2023 · all stores closed, 2025  

## 111 · The score that was treated as proof

<sub>**112** — CASE 4 OF 5</sub>

WHAT HAPPENED  
Australian Catholic University ran Turnitin’s AI-writing detector on student work. Turnitin itself warns the score may be wrong and should never be the only basis for action. Staff often acted on the score alone. One paramedic student was accused of cheating because the tool flagged 84% of his essay.  
WHAT IT COST  
Nearly 6,000 alleged misconduct cases in 2024, about 90% of them about AI (the university says those figures overstate it). One nursing student had her results withheld for six months before she was cleared; she believes it cost her a graduate job. The university knew of problems for over a year before it dropped the tool in March 2025.  
WHAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT  
Deciding before launch that a score can start a conversation but never end one — and that a person gathers the evidence.  
A detector score is not evidence. The vendor said so first.  
ABC News investigation, October 2025  

## 112 · The spreadsheet pasted into ChatGPT

<sub>**113** — CASE 5 OF 5</sub>

WHAT HAPPENED  
A temporary staff member at a New South Wales government agency uploaded an Excel spreadsheet about applicants to a flood-recovery housing programme into a personal ChatGPT account — more than 12,000 rows. It broke the agency’s own IT policy, and nobody noticed for months.  
WHAT IT COST  
2,031 flood victims’ names, addresses, dates of birth and health details left the agency. It took about seven months to disclose. The agency paid for identity protection and counselling referrals, ordered an independent review, and now blocks personal data from AI tools. No sign yet that anyone else saw it.  
WHAT WOULD HAVE PREVENTED IT  
One question before pasting: is any of this someone else’s to give away? Take the names out, or use the tool your organisation has approved.  
Nothing was hacked. One upload was enough.  
NSW Reconstruction Authority breach notice · reported by iTnews, October 2025  

## 113 · Five cases, five names

<sub>**114** — NOW GIVE IT A NAME</sub>

You have already met every one of these ideas. These are the words everyone else uses for them.  
Case 1 · Telangana ration cards  
Fairness  
A wrong data match decided who lost their rations — and nobody checked it.  
Case 2 · South Africa’s AI policy  
Accountability  
A Cabinet signature sat on sources that no human had opened.  
Case 3 · Rite Aid facial recognition  
Transparency  
Staff acted on alerts without ever being told how often those alerts were wrong.  
Case 4 · The AI-cheating detector  
Human oversight  
A score became a verdict, though the vendor said it must not.  
Case 5 · The flood-victims spreadsheet  
Privacy  
The data left the building before anyone had decided that it could.  
Reliability and safety sits under all five — a system that works in a demo is not a system that works on a Tuesday.  

## 114 · Notice what is missing from all five

<sub>**115** — FIVE CASES, ONE PATTERN</sub>

Nobody was hacked.  
Nobody acted maliciously.  
Nobody was careless in a way they would have called careless.  
In every one, the AI did exactly what it was built to do — and a human trusted it at the one moment when trust was the wrong move.  
SO  Responsible AI is not about controlling the AI. It is about knowing where to put your own judgement.  

## 115 · The rules pull against each other

<sub>**116** — WHY THIS IS HARDER THAN A CHECKLIST</sub>

Anyone who tells you responsible AI is a checklist has not had to apply two of these at the same time.  
FAIRNESS VS PRIVACY  
To prove a system is not biased, you need to know who it failed — gender, ethnicity, age. That is exactly the data you were told not to collect.  
TRANSPARENCY VS SAFETY  
Publish how the fraud check works and you have published how to pass it. Full openness is not automatically the responsible setting.  
ACCURACY VS EXPLAINABILITY  
The model you can explain is rarely the one that performs best. Somebody has to choose between them — and be able to say why.  
You are not being asked to resolve these. You are being asked to notice which one you just traded away — and to be able to say so out loud.  

## 116 · Your skill has defaults, and they are not neutral

<sub>**117** — THE ONE YOU BUILT IN PART 4</sub>

You wrote its instructions. You did not write what it already believed before you opened it.  
Every model arrives with a worldview baked in. Yours arrived with one too — you just did not choose it.  
Trained mostly in English, mostly on Western text  
Ask it about Nepali labour law, local salary bands or a Kathmandu supplier and it answers with the same confidence it uses for California.  
It has a house voice you did not pick  
Corporate, hedged, faintly American. If you never specify one, that quietly becomes your organisation’s voice.  
It fills gaps rather than leaving them  
Saying nothing is not in its training. An empty field comes back plausible instead of coming back empty.  
TEST IT  Ask your skill something you already know the local answer to. Whatever it gets wrong there, it is getting wrong everywhere you cannot check.  

## 117 · Do you have to say it was AI?

<sub>**118** — THE QUESTION NOBODY ASKS OUT LOUD</sub>

Not a legal answer. A rule you can hold when a client asks you directly, in the room, with no warning.  
NO NEED TO SAY IT  
AI helped you think, search, restructure or tidy your own words. It was a tool the way a spellchecker is a tool. Nobody needs a footnote for that.  
SAY IT PLAINLY  
AI produced substance you are presenting as your own analysis — findings, figures, recommendations, a draft you only lightly edited.  
YOU MUST SAY IT  
Anyone downstream would decide differently if they knew. Client deliverables, research, assessments, anything carrying your signature.  
The test is not “did I use AI.” It is “would they feel misled to find out.”  
Disclosure is the one duty in this part that no tool setting can handle for you.  

## 118 · The rules are arriving, and they arrive at you

<sub>**119** — THIS IS NO LONGER JUST GOOD MANNERS</sub>

Nepal approved its first National AI Policy in August 2025. You need to know these exist — your clients already do.  
EU AI ACT  
The first broad AI law. It sorts systems by risk, and anything touching hiring, credit, education or essential services carries duties: documentation, human oversight, disclosure. Duties phase in from 2025 to 2028; the main high-risk ones now start in December 2027.  
ISO/IEC 42001  
The management-system standard for AI. This is what an auditor asks for when a client wants proof that you govern AI rather than proof that you say you do.  
YOUR CLIENT’S CONTRACT  
Arriving fastest of the three, and quietly. AI clauses in service agreements and vendor questionnaires are already routine — they did not wait for any legislation.  
Their first three questions are the ones you just practised: what did the AI do, who checked it, and whose name is on it.  

## 119 · What not to put in — and what to put in instead

<sub>**120** — THE ONE THAT CATCHES EVERYONE</sub>

Not a legal definition. A working one, for the things that actually cross your desk.  
NEVER PASTE THE REAL THING  
PASTE THIS INSTEAD  
Contracts, and their commercial terms  
The one clause you are asking about, with names and figures replaced  
ID or tax numbers, bank and card details  
Nothing. There is no version of this you need  
Salary, appraisal or disciplinary records  
The question with the person taken out of it  
Health records, or anything said in confidence  
The situation described in general terms  
Passwords, API keys, internal source code  
A minimal example that reproduces the problem  
Unreleased financials, board papers, audit findings  
Dummy figures of the same order of magnitude  
You almost never need the real data. You need the shape of the problem.  And check your training setting once. Ninety seconds.  

## 120 · There are only two moments that matter

<sub>**121** — BEFORE YOU ACT ON ANYTHING</sub>

Everything else in an AI task is typing. These are the two points where a decision is actually available to you.  
**1** — Before you paste  
Is any of this someone else’s to give away?  
Yours is your business. Your customer’s, your patient’s, your colleague’s is not yours to spend. If the answer is yes, replace it before you press enter — you almost never needed the real thing.  
THIS IS THE ONE THAT PREVENTED CASE 5  
**2** — Before you act  
Is there a name, a number, a date or a citation in here?  
Then check that one thing against the source — not against the AI. Asking it to check its own work is not checking. It will confirm its own invention in the same confident tone.  
THIS IS THE ONE THAT PREVENTED CASE 2  
Between those two moments, do whatever you like. Outside them, you are the only control there is. Neither takes eight seconds. Both take about one.  

## 121 · Who is allowed to decide what

<sub>**122** — IF YOU REMEMBER ONE THING</sub>

The rule that survives every tool, every model and every version number.  
THE TASK  
AI MAY  
A NAMED HUMAN MUST  
Summarising, drafting, restructuring, translating  
do all of it  
read it before it leaves  
Anything with a figure, a date or a citation in it  
produce it  
verify it against the source  
Anything sent outside the organisation  
draft it  
approve it, and send it  
Anything that changes a person’s outcome — hiring, discipline, credit, admission, a claim  
inform the decision  
make and own the decision, by name  
This is not a brake on any of it. It is the reason any of it can go in front of a real customer.

## 124 · Three questions to answer for yourself

<sub>**125** — TAKE THREE MINUTES</sub>

Write them down. Nobody will read them out — which is the only reason an honest answer is possible.  
**1** — Where am I using AI to think better — and where am I using it to stop thinking?  
Using it to structure an argument is thinking better. Using it so that you never have to form one is not. Same tool, same afternoon. Which were you, this week?  
**2** — Where have I quietly stopped checking?  
Everyone has one place where it has been right often enough that you stopped looking. An email. A summary. A number. Name yours — that is where your version of the six invented cases is waiting.  
**3** — What have I put into it that wasn’t mine to share?  
A classmate’s draft. A client’s contract. A colleague’s salary. A patient’s name. A friend’s message. Probably without a second’s thought.  
AND THEN  Pick the one that made you uncomfortable. That is the one worth changing this week — not all three.

## 129 · Send the HOLD back

<sub>**99** — THE LOOP  ·  FIX AND RECHECK</sub>

The Checker said what is wrong and how to fix it. Give that to the Writer.  
**1** — Copy the Checker’s whole answer  
Every verdict, with each FIX.  
**2** — Open a new chat. Type /writer  
Paste your drafts, then the Checker’s answer.  
**3** — The Writer fixes only the HOLDs  
It applies each FIX and marks the result ROUND 2.  
**4** — New chat. Type /checker. Paste. Send.  
Round 2 is the last round.  
The Writer still writes. The Checker still flags. Only the baton goes back.  

## 130 · Two rounds, then a human

<sub>**100** — THE STOPPING RULE</sub>

A loop needs an exit. Without one, two workers can pass the same problem back and forth forever.  
ROUND 1  The Writer drafts  →  the Checker flags, and writes a FIX.  
ROUND 2  The Writer applies the FIX  →  the Checker looks again. Still HOLD? HAND TO A HUMAN.  
IF ROUND 2 SAYS SEND  
Did it fix the problem, or just the wording? The refund is unsettled until someone checks the chalan.  
IF ROUND 2 STILL SAYS HOLD  
No round 3. The Checker writes HAND TO A HUMAN, and the draft goes to its owner.  
Some HOLDs can’t be fixed by rewriting. The fix is a person checking the chalan.  

## 131 · It reads the whole chat. Every time.

<sub>**104** — WHAT IT COSTS</sub>

WHAT YOU NOTICE  
A long chat gets slower. A rule you set at the top starts to slip. The free plan asks you to come back later.  
And all you typed was four words: “make it shorter.”  
WHAT IS HAPPENING  
Before every answer, it reads the whole chat again: the skill’s instructions, its files, the transcript, every draft, every reply.  
Your four words sit at the bottom of all that, and all of it is read again.  
IT HAS A NAME  Tokens: the small pieces of text it reads and writes. A chat’s room, and its cost, are counted in them.  

## 132 · Three ways to make it read less

<sub>**105** — SPEND FEWER TOKENS</sub>

You have been doing all three today. Now you know why.  
New chat  
One chat per job. That is why every worker started fresh: /listener, /writer, /checker.  
Only what it needs  
The Writer got the register, not the transcript. Paste the part that matters, not the whole file.  
Ask for less back  
“A table. Nothing else.” Your Listener already says it. A short answer costs less.  
Less to read means a faster answer, more room before you hit a limit, and rules at the top that still get followed.  
ONE MORE THING  A skill saves your typing, not its reading. Its instructions are read again every time you call it, so keep them short.  

## 133 · Same five dials, different labels

<sub>**65** — YOU WILL SEE THESE EVERYWHERE</sub>

Every prompt template you find online is a version of what you just did. Read each one against your five dials.  
STAR · Situation, Task, Action, Result  
Source, Shape  
Borrowed from job interviews. No Role, and nothing about what to do when a fact is missing.  
CO-STAR · Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience, Response  
Source, Role, Shape, Style  
Splits your Style dial into style and tone. No Limits.  
RTF · Role, Task, Format  
Role, Shape  
The minimum. Fine for a quick question, thin for anything you will act on.  
RISEN · Role, Instructions, Steps, End goal, Narrowing  
Role, Shape, Limits  
Narrowing is your Limits dial. Steps is the Part 4 idea. No Source.  
Google’s guide · Persona, Task, Context, Format  
Role, Source, Shape  
Google’s own prompting guide for Gemini. No Style, no Limits.  
The one thing almost none of them include: an example. Show it one good answer and it copies the shape.
